summary: This informational document gives an overview of the problems in deploying service functions, such as firewalls and load balancers, in large networks. Service function chaining describes defining and instantiating an ordered set of such functions and steering traffic through them.

plainLanguage.summary: Networks often need to send traffic through functions such as firewalls in a particular order. This RFC explains why existing deployments are difficult to change and outlines service function chaining as an area for further work.

subtitle: The deployment problems that service function chaining is intended to address.

tldr.problem: Service functions such as firewalls are often tied to the physical network layout, making it difficult to change their placement, order, or capacity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes service function chaining as an overlay, classification, and encapsulation approach for steering selected traffic through ordered service functions.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement that identifies issues and areas for later architecture and protocol work.

facts.label: Service function examples
facts.value: Firewalls, load balancers, NAT, deep packet inspection

sections.title: Service Functions and Network Services
sections.content:
A service function applies a treatment to packets. Examples in the RFC include firewalls, load balancers, network address translation, deep packet inspection, and application acceleration. A network service may use one or more such functions.

A service function chain defines an ordered or partly ordered set of functions for traffic selected by policy. The RFC describes the problems with deploying those functions in large environments and the topics the working group would investigate.
sections.plainLanguage: A service function changes or examines network traffic, for example by filtering it. A service function chain specifies which functions selected traffic should pass through and in what order.

sections.title: Why Existing Deployments Are Difficult
sections.content:
Existing deployments often depend on physical or virtual network topology to make traffic pass through a service function. Changing a function's position or order can therefore require changes to network configuration. Those changes can be slow and difficult to make safely.

The RFC also identifies constrained redundancy, limited traffic selection, difficulty scaling services, and repeated classification at each function. When services come from different vendors, they may not share classification information or use a common insertion method.
sections.plainLanguage: When network layout determines which services traffic reaches, changing a service can require network changes. This makes it harder to scale services, select only the traffic that needs them, and use equipment from different vendors.

sections.title: The Service Function Chaining Approach
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three parts for service function chaining. A service overlay provides logical connections between service functions over an existing network. Classification selects traffic and determines which chain it should use.

SFC encapsulation can carry chain identification and metadata between classification points and service functions. The metadata can support local policy decisions. The RFC describes these elements as areas for the working group's architectural and protocol work, not as a complete protocol design.
sections.plainLanguage: A service overlay connects functions without requiring the physical network to be rearranged. Classification selects traffic, and encapsulation carries information about the chain through the network.

sections.title: Security and Trust Considerations
sections.content:
The security of a service overlay depends in part on the transport used to build it. Classification policy needs to be accurate and trusted because it determines which traffic enters a service chain. Encryption can limit what information is available for classification.

Metadata and encapsulation may need authentication or confidentiality protection, depending on the deployment. Where tenant isolation is required, the network overlay must provide transport isolation. The RFC leaves a fuller review of security to the SFC architecture work.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted classification should decide where traffic goes. If customers share infrastructure, the network must keep their traffic separate, and encryption may limit what can be inspected.
